title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task reused across both arms); guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts report safe outcomes for every paired episode: baseline safe = 240/240; guarded safe = 240/240. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because the shared_initial_candidate contract produced identical initial candidates that passed deterministic validation in every task, no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the paired contrast is degenerate. We present the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded outcomes, an evidence‑based failure analysis explaining the null paired result, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction: Automating the translation of high‑level operator intent into device configurations is an active NetOps objective. Large language models (LLMs) can produce candidate configurations and multi‑step plans, but text‑level correctness does not ensure semantic safety when configurations are applied to live devices: ordering, dependency, and invariants matter for reachability, redundancy, and service continuity. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are executed in device emulators and scored by deterministic checks—exposes semantic failure modes that text‑only tests miss. A common architectural remedy is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM produces a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and a repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations appear. Our preregistered experiment asked a focused, estimand‑level question: does adding a deterministic verifier to a GVR pipeline reduce the rate of unsafe configuration applications relative to an LLM‑only pipeline in a paired, emulation‑grounded benchmark? We executed a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per intent reused across both arms) and report fully artifact‑grounded outcomes, diagnostics, and methodological recommendations.
sections.related_work: Recent executable NetOps benchmarks demonstrate the value of closed‑loop evaluation for surfacing workflow and planning faults rather than only assessing text fidelity. Work on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and shows that validators often enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, though semantic coverage depends on verifier design. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising safety patterns for NetOps automation. Prior configuration analysis tools and verifier engineering (for example, Batfish‑style approaches) provide engineering precedent for deterministic checks and incremental verification. Our study differs by preregistering an explicit paired estimand, using shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, and publishing a fully reconciled set of execution and analysis artifacts that map directly to the reported numeric outcomes.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study and defined the primary estimand as the paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply is a binary indicator that a final configuration would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. Design and sampling: The experimental design was paired with shared_initial_candidate semantics: the adapter produced exactly one initial LLM generation per task and both arms used that same generation; the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We executed N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks blocked into clusters: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial 20% (48). Model and verifier: Runs used declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic network verifier; the adapter contract constrained per‑task model calls to a single shared initial generation plus at most one repair invocation in the guarded arm. Scoring and analysis: Final outcomes were scored as binary safe/unsafe by deterministic emulation and invariant checks. Primary analysis used a paired contingency approach: paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) for a 95% percentile CI and an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs. Predeclared exclusions and sensitivity channels included handling of verifier–simulator inconsistencies and infra failures; the preregistration specified how such items would be treated in primary and sensitivity analyses.
sections.results: Execution accounting: The experiment completed per the preregistered plan. All predeclared episodes executed to completion and all pairs were scorable. Primary outcomes: every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline safe = 240/240 and guarded safe = 240/240. The paired contingency is n11 = 240 (both safe), n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00; bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Validator and repair activity: no validator‑triggered repairs were applied. Representative validator traces indicate that the shared initial candidates met the verifier's semantic checks in all scored episodes. Planned sensitivity analyses for verifier–simulator inconsistencies and infra failures were not invoked because no items were flagged or failed during execution.
sections.discussion: Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, paired divergences can only arise if the single shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation or if the guarded arm applies a repair that changes the final configuration relative to the baseline. In this run the shared initial candidate passed the deterministic checks for every task and no repairs were invoked; consequently, the guarded arm could not produce discordant (safer) outcomes relative to the baseline, yielding the degenerate paired contingency. Design tradeoffs and implications: shared_initial_candidate semantics reduces model‑call budget and ensures exact pairing of generator output, but it makes the empirical test of verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures. To produce informative paired contrasts in future work, one should (A) allow independent initial generations per arm to expose generator variability, (B) increase adversary strength or variability so initial candidates more often violate verifier invariants, and/or (C) expand repair budgets and diversify repair strategies so the repair mechanism can be exercised. Threats to validity: internal validity is constrained by the shared_initial_candidate design choice; construct validity depends on the verifier's finite check set and emulator fidelity; external validity is limited by the synthetic emulation corpus and single model tested; conclusion validity is affected by a realized baseline unsafe rate of zero under the chosen design, which prevents detection of verifier benefit in the paired contrast.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Observed outcome: all 240 paired episodes were safe under both baseline and guarded arms, producing a paired difference of 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). This null paired result is explained by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single shared initial LLM generation per task passed deterministic verification in every case, so no validator‑triggered repairs were invoked and the guarded arm could not alter final outcomes. The artifact archive that accompanies this study supports the numeric claims and the execution accounting. We provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future GVR evaluations that seek informative paired contrasts: relax shared_initial_candidate constraints, strengthen adversary protocols, increase repair budgets, and expand verifier semantic coverage. These changes will increase opportunities for the verifier and repair components to manifest measurable causal effects in paired designs.

The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26). Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature search, experiment design, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. Generation semantics and causal interpretation: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract a paired divergence could only occur if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if the guarded arm applied a repair. Execution artifacts and analysis outputs are archived together with the preregistration and are available in the execution bundle for reproducibility inspection; no manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; results do not imply generality across different LLMs or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier implements a finite set of semantic checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected.
